text: Beneath the desk lamp, the cursor blinks at the end of a sentence I wrote an hour ago, and I cannot tell whether it is finished. My coffee has gone cold beside the keyboard. I read the same paragraph three times before my eyes stop skipping over the words.

Our team meeting ends and everyone stands up at once, but I stay in my chair with the laptop still open. The reminder about the budget form pops up in the corner of the screen. I watch it, then close it, then open it again without reading what it says.

Before lunch the inbox holds forty-one unread messages, and I have answered none of them. I type a reply to Lena, delete it, and type a shorter one. My hand rests on the mouse for a while before the click happens.

Down the corridor from the elevator, I walk the length of the third floor the way I walk up a hill. Printer paper sits in a stack beside the copier. I pick up one sheet, put it down, and pick up the next.

Onions hiss in the pan and I know I should stir them, but the spoon stays in its drawer. A pot of rice sits on the back burner with its lid rattling. Eventually I turn the flame down and sit on the stool beside the stove.

Breakfast is a bowl of oats I spooned out a while ago and have not touched since. A thin skin has formed across the top. I pick up the honey jar, turn it over in my fingers, and set it back on the counter without opening it.

Dinner guests have finished their plates, and the candles down the table have burned to puddles of wax. Someone asks for the bread and I pass the basket, but my arm stays on the cloth long after the basket has gone. Nobody notices, and I keep my eyes on the empty dish in front of me.

Flour dusts the recipe card propped against the canister, and I have read the second step four times without seeing it. I know how to fold egg whites. Still, the bowl sits on the counter, the whisk untouched beside it, and I lean on the cupboard door.

Ahead of me the light turns green, and the car behind honks, but I sit with both hands on the wheel and leave the pedal alone. My mind goes blank on a route I have driven every weekday for years. I have to glance at a street sign to remember which turn comes next.

Just as I reach the curb, the bus pulls away from the stop, and I watch its tail lights shrink down the avenue. Rain runs off the edge of the shelter roof in a thin sheet. I shift my bag higher on my shoulder and stay where I am, reading the timetable twice before the letters hold still.

On the train platform I let the first two trains go by, though they are the ones I always take. The doors close with a chime that sounds like it is coming through water. Only when the next one slows do I lift my bag from the floor and step toward the yellow line.

Somewhere past the exit the gas light comes on, and I keep meaning to stop at the station. My fingers find the turn signal and leave it alone. Cars pass me on the left, and I let them go, watching the white line slide under the hood without deciding anything.

Halfway up the hill I stop on a flat rock with my pack still on, and the wind pushes at my jacket. Below me the river moves with a steady sound, like pages turning in another room. A jay lands on the fence post and watches me, and I watch it back without lifting my camera.

Frost covers the garden beds, and the hose lies coiled where I dropped it yesterday. I pick up the nozzle, then set it on the step again. Sparrows argue in the hedge while I crouch over the first bean leaves pushing through the mulch.

Across the lake a canoe drifts past the reeds, its paddle resting across the seats. I sit on the dock with my feet in the water, which is cold enough to notice. A dragonfly lands on my knee and stays there, and I let it, because getting up would take more effort than I want to spend.

Faded trail markers leave me unsure whether the blue ones point this way or the other. I sit on a fallen log and eat a handful of nuts from my pocket, one at a time. Pine needles crunch when a squirrel runs across the path, and I listen to it go without getting up to see where it went.

Clean laundry waits in its basket by the dryer, with a towel hanging over one edge. I know the shirts belong in the second drawer, but I hold a pile of socks in the bedroom doorway and cannot begin. Dust turns in the light from the window while I wait for my feet to move.

Since before lunch I have been looking at the vacuum cord, wrapped around its handle in neat loops. Crumbs gather under the kitchen table where the morning cereal spilled. I kneel to pick up the largest piece, then sit back on my heels with it in my palm.

Dishes stack on the drainboard, a glass rim catching the afternoon sun. I know the order I usually wash them in, but I cannot get my hands to start with the pot. Water drips from the tap at an even pace, and I count the drops for a while.

Yesterday's streak still marks the bathroom mirror, even though I wiped it. I fold the towel in half, then in half again, and hang it on the rack. Floorboards creak overhead under the bare feet of someone upstairs, and I stop to listen.

My number has not appeared on the waiting room screen, and the clock above the desk says twenty to three. I fill in the clipboard form and read each question twice before I can answer it. The receptionist has spelled my surname wrong on the sheet, and it takes me a while to notice.

A nurse asks me to roll up my sleeve, and I manage the button on the second try. The blood pressure cuff tightens around my arm and then lets go with a hiss. She writes something on the chart, and I watch her pen move across the paper without asking what it says.

At the physiotherapy clinic, the therapist asks me to lift my leg onto the bench. I have done this exercise at home every morning for a month. Today the instructions in my head arrive late, after my leg has already started or stopped, and I cannot tell which.

Behind the pharmacy counter, a pharmacist asks for my date of birth, and I know it by heart. The answer takes a moment to surface, and I say it twice to be sure. Then I wait on the bench with the paper bag on my knees, watching the screen above the register for my name.

While I fold towels on the bed, my sister calls and I put the phone on speaker. She tells me about her new job, and I say the right things at the right times. Halfway through a story I realize I have lost track of which of her children is which.

Cards are fanned across my friend's kitchen table, and the deal comes around to me. I look at my hand, and the suits blur together. Ana asks whether it is my turn, so I nod and pick a card at random without sorting the rest.

Once again the story about the boat comes up after dinner, and I know the ending before anyone reaches it. I sit at the end of the couch with a plate on my knee. When everyone laughs, I laugh a beat late, after the room has already moved on.

Candles flicker on the birthday cake while the room sings, and my voice arrives thin and out of step. I know every word of the song. My cousin passes me a slice on a paper plate, and I hold it on my lap long after the frosting has started to soften.

Open to chapter seven, the textbook shows the diagram of cells I drew twice last month. I read the caption, then read it again, and the words stay flat on the page. My pencil rolls off the desk, and I leave it lying on the floor.

Floor polish hangs in the air of the exam hall, and the clock ticks loudly above the whiteboard. I know the formula for the area of a circle, but the symbols on the paper look unfamiliar. I write my name at the top, then sit with the pen hovering above the first question.

Silence settles over the seminar room, and the professor's gaze moves along the rows toward me. The answer is somewhere in my head, like a word on the tip of the tongue, but reaching for it takes too long. A classmate offers a hint, and I nod and copy it into my notes.

Dried out, my highlighter leaves no mark under the library lamp, which buzzes above the table. I have reread the same paragraph about the French revolution four times, taking in each sentence without keeping any of it. I turn the page, and the next one looks just as long.

Nearly empty, the track holds one man walking a dog on the far side. I start the warm-up jog, and my legs take the first lap in a late, uneven rhythm. I know my usual pace by heart, but the watch shows a number I do not expect, so I slow to a walk on the curve.

Under the bed a yoga mat has waited for weeks, and I drag it out across the living room floor. The video instructor asks me to breathe into my hips, and I know this pose well. My arms stay at my sides while the video moves on to the next position without me.

Children shriek in the swimming pool, and the lane ropes sway from the current. I push off the wall, and my arms move through the water the way they always do. Halfway down the lane I stop, hang onto the rope, and watch the tiles on the bottom slide slowly beneath me.

Grinding has come from the bicycle chain all week, and I still have not oiled it. I wheel the bike to the door, swing one leg over the seat, and rest there with both feet on the ground. My gym bag hangs off the handlebars, and I leave it swinging.

Beside a box of spare screws, the screwdriver rests in my palm. The chair leg wobbles every time I shift my weight, and I know exactly which screw goes in the corner hole. My fingers stay open, and the screwdriver rolls a few inches across the table before I stop it.

Clay on the wheel has stiffened at the edges, and the vase I was shaping has slumped to one side. I remember how to center it, my palms steady and even. Today my hands press too hard, and I let the wheel slow and stop without reaching for the sponge.

Wood glue is open on the workbench, and the two boards sit clamped and waiting. I have glued a hundred joints like this one. I spread the glue along the edge, then stop and watch the wet line creep across the grain.

Threaded and ready, the sewing machine waits beside fabric pinned flat with white chalk lines. I know how to start a straight stitch. The pedal sits under my foot, and for a long moment I keep my foot exactly where it is.

Pulling left, my cart drifts down the supermarket aisle under flat white light. My list has five items and I have found only two. I slow in front of the cereal boxes and read them from top to bottom without choosing one.

Clerks at the post office stamp each parcel with a slow, even thump. I hold a padded envelope against my chest and check the address on it twice. When my turn comes, I hand it over and forget what the stamp cost.

Hardware store shelves have been moved, and the bolts I came for now sit in a different aisle. I walk the aisles with a basket on my arm, reading the labels slowly. I find the right drawer in the end, but I cannot remember how I got there.

Handing back my card, the bank teller asks whether I need anything else. The question seems to take a long time to reach me. I shake my head, then stand by the door for a moment before I remember which way is out.

Hotel key cards fail on the first try, and a green light blinks at me from the lock. I wait in the hallway, knowing the room number, though it takes a while to recall which floor I am on. Somewhere past that door my suitcase sits half unpacked from last night.

Gate numbers change twice on the screen above the departure lounge. I know my seat number, yet I read the boarding pass three times before I understand which row it is. A child runs past with a red balloon, and I follow it with my eyes until the crowd closes over it.

Out of the coastal station, a train slides away, and the window fills with flat fields and one line of poplars. My ticket is folded in my lap, and I have not taken out my book. A woman across the aisle offers me a biscuit, and I take it, then hold it without eating.

Folded to the wrong side, the map shows street names that mean nothing to me. The guidebook says the market is ten minutes away, but I have walked for twenty. Church bells ring somewhere behind the rooftops, and I keep my pace slow at each crossing.

With the piano lid up and the sonata open on its stand, I sit down at the bench. I know this piece well enough to play it with my eyes closed. My fingers rest on the keys without pressing, and the room stays silent while the metronome keeps ticking.

Dropping from the brush, a bead of water lands on the paper and spreads into a grey circle. I meant to paint the hills at dusk. The colors I mixed earlier have dried on the palette, and I leave them there.

Resting across my knees, the guitar holds the chord I need in my head. My hand does not move to make it. Outside, the neighbor's dog barks twice, then stops, and I listen to the quiet until the strings start to feel like someone else's.

Knitting needles lie crossed on the sofa cushion with a half-finished sleeve hanging from them. I know the pattern by heart and could knit it in my sleep. Tonight the stitches will not count themselves, and I sit with the yarn in my lap while the television murmurs.

Frozen again, the spreadsheet on my laptop sits under a whirring fan. I know the shortcut to save it, but my finger hovers over the key and then withdraws. A small spinning wheel keeps turning while I watch it.

Notifications buzz across my phone, one from the bank and another from a muted group chat. I pick it up to reply and open the wrong app. I stare at the home screen for a while, the icons swimming in front of me, before I lock it again.

An email about my password reset arrives with a link that I click. The next screen wants a six-digit code from my authenticator app. I know which app it is, but the number changes before I can type it, so I try again, and it changes again.

Blinking orange in the hallway, the printer has its paper tray hanging open. I know how to clear a jam, and I have done it before. I reach for the lever, pause with my hand on the warm metal, and let the light keep blinking.
